report:
### Conclusion
Your expectation aligns with the scientific consensus: **there is no clear, reliable evidence that hypnosis is an effective standalone treatment for smoking cessation.**

### Summary of Evidence

* **Lack of Superior Efficacy:** The primary gold-standard evaluation comes from Cochrane Systematic Reviews analyzing randomized controlled trials. Researchers concluded that there is no clear evidence hypnotherapy produces higher long-term quit rates (at 6 months or longer) than brief advice, placebo, or other behavioral interventions (https://www.cochrane.org/th/evidence/CD001008_does-hypnotherapy-help-people-who-are-trying-stop-smoking; https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/31198991/). If any specific benefit exists, evidence indicates it is small at best.
* **Mixed and Inconsistent Research:** A meta-analysis of hypnosis literature noted that while individual trials occasionally report positive short-term outcomes, overall effects vary widely and are often undermined by small sample sizes and methodological limitations (https://www.frontiersin.org/journals/psychology/articles/10.3389/fpsyg.2023.1330238/full).
* **Potential as an Adjunct Only:** Health resources note that while hypnosis may aid general relaxation or assist individual motivation when combined with broader lifestyle interventions, current evidence does not justify recommending it over proven methods (https://www.healthline.com/health/hypnosis-to-quit-smoking).

First-line, evidence-based treatments with proven long-term success remain cognitive-behavioral counseling and approved cessation medications (such as nicotine replacement therapy or varenicline).
